title: Wearable headset-assisted fluoroscopic visualization during complex endovascular aortic repair
text:
## INNOVATIVE TECHNIQUES

## Wearable headset-assisted fluoroscopic visualization during complex endovascular aortic repair

Dai Yamanouchi, MD, PhD, EMBA, a,b Toyoake, Japan; and Madison, WI

ABSTRACT 
Complex endovascular aortic repair (EVAR) frequently requires simultaneous femoral and upper-extremity access, 
particularly during multibranched endograft implantation, branched thoracic EVAR, and other procedures requiring 
target-vessel catheterization from the arm. In hybrid operating rooms, the arm-side operator often has a limited or 
obstructed view of the primary fluoroscopy monitor because of the image intensifier, patient position, equipment, 
radiation shielding, or distance from the main display. Although secondary monitors can be used, they may be small, 
poorly positioned, or difficult to align with the operator’s working angle. We describe a simple wearable headset 
assisted fluoroscopic visualization technique using commercially available components, including XREAL One Pro 
glasses (XREAL, Inc), a wireless high-definition multimedia interface transmission module, and a digital visual interface 
to-high-definition multimedia interface connector. The system allows the live fluoroscopic image to be displayed as an 
individualized virtual monitor within the operator’s field of view while preserving awareness of the operative field 
through a see-through display and adjustable shading. The headset can provide a stable three-degree-of-freedom or 
six-degree-of-freedom image as needed. This technique may be particularly useful for the arm-side operator during 
multibranch endograft procedures or branched thoracic EVAR, where precise wire, catheter, sheath, and bridging stent 
manipulation is required. Wearable headset-assisted fluoroscopic visualization may simplify hybrid operating room 
setup, reduce dependence on monitor positioning, and improve operator ergonomics. Further evaluation is needed to 
assess its effect on procedure efficiency, fluoroscopy time, radiation exposure, operator workload, and safety. (J Vasc 
Surg Cases Innov Tech 2026;12:102385.) 
Keywords: Endovascular surgery; Complexed aortic aneurysm; Vascular surgery 

Complex endovascular aortic repair (EVAR) has advanced rapidly with the development of fenestrated, branched, and multibranched endograft technologies. These procedures frequently require simultaneous ac cess from the femoral and upper-extremity routes, particularly when target-vessel catheterization, branch cannulation, or bridging stent deployment is performed from the brachial or axillary approach. In these settings, the arm-side operator must perform delicate wire, cath eter, and sheath manipulation while continuously moni toring fluoroscopic imaging. 1-3 However, optimal fluoroscopic visualization is often difficult for the arm-side operator. In many hybrid oper ating room configurations, the main fluoroscopy monitor is positioned primarily for the femoral operator.

The arm-side operator may be located away from the main monitor, behind the image intensifier, or in a posi tion where the monitor is partially obstructed by the C arm, radiation shields, anesthesia equipment, sterile ta bles, or other operating room components. Although secondary or “slave” monitors can be used, they are often smaller, less optimally positioned, or difficult to align with the operator’s working angle. This limitation becomes particularly important during multibranched thoracoabdominal endograft procedures and branched thoracic EVAR (TEVAR), in which small wire and catheter movements must be interpreted in real time. 3 Even subtle loss of visualization can interfere with safe and efficient can nulation, sheath advancement, and bridging stent deployment. Head-mounted displays, smart glasses, and augmented-reality technologies have been increasingly explored in surgery. A systematic review of head mounted display use in surgery described broad applica tions across multiple surgical specialties, including image display, surgical navigation, education, and telementor ing. 4 In vascular surgery, Lareyre et al 5 reviewed applica tions of head-mounted displays and smart glasses and noted that available studies largely represent early proof-of-concept applications in education, simulation, telemedicine, and intraoperative assistance. review of augmented reality in vascular and endovascular surgery similarly emphasized that the field remains early but potentially relevant to endovascular visualization and workflow. 6 Previous reports have described more advanced holo graphic or augmented-reality applications in endovas cular surgery. Rynio et al 7 reported holographically guided endovascular aneurysm repair using augmented-reality visualization of vascular anatomy during EVAR. Mialhe et al 8 also evaluated the feasibility of using a Microsoft HoloLens head-mounted display (Microsoft Corporation) during endovascular surgery. The present technique differs from these navigation focused approaches. Rather than using the wearable headset for image registration, holographic anatomy projection, or procedural navigation, this method uses commercially available wearable display glasses as a personal fluoroscopy monitor. The goal is to improve intraoperative visualization and ergonomics, particularly for operators working from the arm side during complex EVAR.

TECHNIQUE The wearable headset fluoroscopy display system con sists of commercially available components: XREAL One Pro glasses (weight 87 g, XREAL, Inc) (Fig 1, A), a high definition multimedia interface (HDMI) to universal se rial bus type-C converter (Fig 1, B), a wireless HDMI trans mission module (Fig 1, C), and a digital visual interface to-HDMI connector (Fig 1, D). The fluoroscopy image output from the hybrid operating room imaging system is connected to the wireless HDMI transmitter through the digital visual interface-to-HDMI converter. The wire less HDMI receiver is then connected to the wearable headset, allowing the live fluoroscopic image to be dis played directly in the operator’s field of view (Fig 2). The cost depends on the region and specific configura tion. In the United States, the wearable glasses are

approximately $600, with additional modest costs for the wireless HDMI module and video adapter. The XREAL One Pro glasses function as a wearable vir tual display. The manufacturer describes the device as providing a micro-OLED display, wide field of view, 1080p visual output (based on HDMI module), adjust able electrochromic dimming, and three-degree-of freedom display stabilization, with six-degree-of freedom capability available using an additional acces sory. These features allow the operator to position the fluoroscopy image as an individualized virtual monitor while maintaining visual awareness of the operative field through the see-through display. Before sterile preparation, the fluoroscopy output signal is connected and confirmed on the wearable headset. The operator adjusts the virtual screen size, po sition, brightness, and shading based on personal prefer ence and the operating room environment. The system is tested before critical procedural steps to confirm im age quality, signal stability, and any perceptible delay compared with the standard fluoroscopy monitor. During the procedure, the wearable headset can be worn by the arm-side operator, femoral operator, assis tant, trainee, or any team member requiring an individ ualized fluoroscopy display. For arm-access procedures, the headset allows the operator to view the live fluoro scopic image without repeatedly turning toward the main monitor or relying on a distant secondary monitor. Because the virtual monitor is individualized, the hybrid operating room monitor arrangement does not need to be substantially modified for each operator. The technique is particularly useful during upper extremity access in complex aortic procedures. During multibranched thoracoabdominal endograft implanta tion, the arm-side operator frequently performs target vessel catheterization and bridging stent delivery while standing near the patient’s arm or shoulder. In this posi tion, the main monitor may be behind the image intensifier or outside the operator’s natural line of sight (Fig 3). With wearable headset-assisted visualization, the operator can maintain a more neutral head position

Fig 2. Schematic of the wearable headset-assisted fluoroscopic visualization system. The live fluoroscopic image output from the hybrid-operating room imaging system is transmitted through a video-output connection to a wireless high-definition multimedia interface (HDMI) transmission module. The signal is then sent wirelessly to the receiver connected to the wearable headset, allowing the operator to view the fluoroscopic image as an individualized virtual display. This setup enables the operator to maintain an un obstructed view of the fluoroscopic image while preserving awareness of the operative field, without requiring repositioning of the conventional operating room monitors.

Fig 3. Conventional visualization challenge for the arm-side operator during complex endovascular aortic repair. In a hybrid operating room, the main fluoroscopy monitor is typically positioned for the femoral-side operator, whereas the arm-side operator may be located near the patient’s upper extremity and partially separated from the main display by the image intensifier, operating table, anesthesia equipment, radiation shields, and other procedural equip ment. As a result, the arm-side operator may need to rely on a smaller submonitor or look across the operative field to ward a distant main monitor, creating an ergonomically unfavorable working position during delicate wire, catheter, sheath, and branch-stent manipulation.

The headset was typically worn during the critical portions of the complex endo vascular procedure, particularly during target-vessel cannulation, branch catheterization, and bridging stent deployment. In selected cases, the operator wore the headset for nearly the entire procedure, depending on operator preference and the need for continuous indi vidualized fluoroscopic visualization. The operator was able to adjust the brightness, position, and shading of the virtual display as needed, which helped maintain image visibility and comfort. Our initial experience was positive, with improved fluoroscopic visibility and less dependence on monitor position.
